READING 11
INTRODUCTION TO FINANCIAL
DATA SCIENCE
MODULE 11.1: INTRODUCTION TO FINANCIAL
DATA SCIENCE
LOS 11.a: Describe how big data, machine learning, and artificial
intelligence are used in financial data science, fintech, and investment
management.
The objective of financial data science is to use quantitative and qualitative
analysis to produce insights into a specific financial matter, such as consumer
behavior patterns or predictions of stock market movements. Three of the main
uses of data analysis techniques in the finance world are (1) evaluation of
investment opportunities, (2) portfolio optimization, and (3) risk mitigation.
The term fintech refers to the meeting of the finance and technology worlds. In
this reading, we focus on fintech developments that aid quantitative analysis
within the investment industry.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
The Level I CFA curriculum recognizes that there are alternative
definitions of fintech, including referring to developments in technology
that can be applied to the financial services industry. Companies that are
in the business of developing technologies for the finance industry are
also often referred to as fintech companies. However, for the Level I
exam, stick to the definition just listed.
Big Data
The foundation of any form of financial data science is data. Big data is a
widely used expression that refers to all the potentially useful information that is

generated. The data collected can be classified as structured, unstructured, or
semi-structured.
Structured data are organized in tables with rows and columns, and typically
stored in a database, such as balance sheet data for companies or records of
market movements.
Unstructured data are not as organized (e.g., data from social media, voice
recordings, pictures, and sensors), making it tricky for a human to effectively
and efficiently deal with the information without assistance in the form of
machine learning algorithms or AI. This often requires specialized computer
programs or code.
Semi-structured data are somewhere in the middle. While they cannot be
stored in a table, they can be tagged and stored in an organized fashion (e.g.,
HTML code).
Regardless of the data format, the first step in analysis is to obtain the relevant
data. Data can come from traditional sources such as financial markets, company
financial reports, and government economic statistics, or from alternative
sources.
Alternative data sources can be categorized as follows:
Individuals. This is social media activity, website activity (such as clicks, time
spent on page, searches), and personal data. The quantity of alternative data
coming from individuals is growing (most of it unstructured).
Business processes. Transaction and corporate data are typically structured,
such as sales information and banking records. Using this data appropriately
can help to give leading or real-time indicators of performance—unlike
traditional business sources, such as quarterly earnings reports, that provide a
lagging view.
Sensors. Devices such as smartphones, smart buildings, connected vehicles,
and satellites can provide unstructured data at vastly higher volumes than either
of the two previous categories. The broad network of such devices is referred
to as the Internet of Things (IoT).
Given the exponentially growing quantity of data produced from nontraditional
sources and the complex process required to convert this information into a
usable format, businesses have emerged that collect, aggregate, and sell this

alternative data. Sellers and buyers need to be mindful of legal and ethical
implications of dealing with this information. Using methods such as web
scraping—the automated extraction of data from websites using specialized tools
—may result in collecting information that is not in the public domain. One of
the key risks is that some of the information captured may be personal and
protected under privacy regulations.
Key characteristics of big data are its volume, velocity, and variety (the “3 Vs”):
The volume of data continues to grow by orders of magnitude. The units in
which data can be measured have increased from megabytes (MB) and
gigabytes (GB) to terabytes (TB) (1,000 gigabytes) and even petabytes (PB)
(1,000 terabytes).
Velocity refers to how quickly data are communicated. Real-time data such as
stock market price feeds are said to have low latency. Data that are only
communicated periodically, or with a lag, have high latency. Generally
speaking, the higher the velocity, the larger the volume of data collected,
increasing from batch collections (typically measured in MB), to periodic
(GB), near real time (TB) and finally, real time (PB).
The variety of data refers to the varying structures in which data may exist. The
more complex the structure, the more storage volume it requires. Variety
ranges from structured forms (tables, typically measured in MB) through to
databases (GB); semi-structured forms like photos, web page code, or audio
files (TB); and unstructured forms like social media, mobile, and video content
(PB).
A fourth “V” is also important when considering financial big data: veracity.
This considers whether the underlying information is reliable and credible. If
not, a user must work to improve these factors before carrying out any analysis.
Taking advantage of big data presents numerous challenges. Analysts must
ensure that the data they use are of high quality, accounting for the possibilities
of outliers, bad or missing data, or sampling biases. The volume of data collected
must be sufficient and appropriate for its intended use.
Data Science
The field of data science concerns how we extract information from big data.
Data science describes methods for processing and visualizing data. Processing

methods include the following:
Capture. This is collecting data and transforming data into usable forms. If
users require low latency, the data need to be presented in real time; otherwise,
slower access may be acceptable.
Curation. This is assuring data quality by adjusting for errors or missing data.
Storage. This is archiving and accessing data. To assess the most appropriate
form of storage, one must consider whether the data are structured, semi-
structured, or unstructured, as well as their latency. Data can be stored in data
lakes, which are centralized repositories capable of storing all three types of
data in their original format.
Search. This is examining stored data to find needed information.
Transfer. This is moving data from their source or a storage medium to the
analytical tool that will use the data. Distributed computing frameworks are
systems that enable data to be processed and analyzed across multiple
machines.
Visualization techniques can help present data in understandable ways. These
techniques include the familiar charts and graphs that display structured data.
Visualizing less structured data requires other methods, such as word clouds that
illustrate the frequency with which words appear in a sample of text; heat maps;
3D graphics; or mind maps that display logical relations between concepts.
The typical information analyzed in financial data science includes stock prices
and trading data, interest and exchange rates, asset returns, accounting data (e.g.,
financial statement analysis and corporate disclosures), and macroeconomic
data. Some of these are high-frequency data (e.g., high-frequency trading,
where data are updated on a millisecond or microsecond basis), while others are
much slower to update, such as corporate disclosures. Financial data science
requires expert knowledge not only in how to handle data, but also in finance to
understand the inputs and outputs of the analysis. Much of the data used is
sequential and time dependent—even cyclical. Methods used to analyze the data
must be able to identify potential issues in the data such as noise, nonstationarity,
interdependencies, or nonlinearity. Some financial data, such as stock
performance, are prone to high probabilities of extreme events (i.e., fat tails).
Other financial data may be harder to analyze due to the low volume available,
such as data originating from emerging markets.

Data mining is one of the main types of data science, focusing on identifying
patterns within large datasets that can then be used to predict outputs. Typically,
this is used on structured data, but as preprocessing methods become more
sophisticated, unstructured data can potentially be converted into a usable format
for this purpose. Pattern identification methods are based on conditional
probabilities (such as Bayes’ theorem) of patterns emerging. One key risk of data
mining is overfitting, where the model misinterprets noise in the data as
important when identifying and extrapolating patterns, rather than excluding it.
Those who deal with financial data must comply with any financial regulatory
requirements. Banks and financial service providers are regulated firms and must
adhere to strict regulations concerning data management, risk assessment, and
model validation. This ensures protection for clients and consumers, alongside
upholding market integrity. Without this, mishandling of the data could, in
extreme circumstances, lead to financial crises.
Even nonregulated firms must ensure they adhere to business law and any
contractual obligations, though they have more flexibility in how they handle
data. As the use of programs and AI grows, users increasingly focus on
thoroughly developing appropriate models, with high levels of testing and
verification. Data privacy is paramount, as is human review and interaction to
ensure any decisions made by models are appropriate.
Machine Learning
In a world with increasing amounts of data available, data science covers the
complex process of collecting, cleaning, modeling, and interpreting the data.
Methods used need to be reliable and allow informed decisions to be made on a
useful time scale, sometimes in real time. Techniques and systems such as
machine learning and AI are growing in use to improve efficiency while
maintaining or improving accuracy compared to human-led analysis.
One of the most prominent subcategories of AI is machine learning (ML). In
ML, a computer algorithm is given inputs of source data, with no assumptions
about their probability distributions, and it may be given outputs of target data.
The algorithm is designed to learn, without human assistance, how to model the
output data based on the input data, or to learn how to detect and recognize
patterns in the input data. The goal is to be able to identify statistically
significant patterns within the data and create predictions as the output.

Interpreting these outputs requires expertise in the subject, whether it is fraud
detection, portfolio optimization, or stock price forecasts.
In supervised learning, the input and output data are labeled, and the machine
learns to model the outputs from the inputs. Then, the machine is given new
data on which to use the model, with the intention of predicting outcomes.
Financial data science is most likely to apply this in uses such as predicting
stock and company performance. Assuming the underlying data are reliable,
this should give accurate results if trained on sufficiently large enough datasets,
but it might not adapt well to new scenarios.
In unsupervised learning, the input data are not labeled, and the machine
learns to describe the structure of the data and identify patterns. No output data
are provided. This can be useful in financial data science for activities like
customer segmentation and anomaly detection. Unsupervised learning is
widely used and understood. It tends to reduce the complexity (dimensionality)
of data, so it can be helpful for exploring data that are otherwise difficult to
analyze.
Reinforcement learning models learn through trial and error and are improved
by providing feedback on their output in the form of rewards or penalties,
which the models use to adjust their analytical techniques. The downside of
this type of ML is that it can take significant training and resources to design a
rewards system that effectively improves the model. Reinforcement learning
has been used well for optimizing portfolios, as it is helpful in sequential
decision-making where it can learn from its past decisions to improve on its
next ones.
Deep learning, sometimes referred to as deep learning nets, is a branch of ML
that uses layers of neural networks (described later in this reading) to identify
patterns, beginning with simple patterns and advancing to more complex ones.
Deep learning may employ supervised, unsupervised, or semi-supervised
learning. Applications of deep learning include image and speech recognition
and natural language processing.
Underfitting is a risk in ML. Underfitting occurs when the machine fails to
identify actual patterns and relationships, treating true parameters as noise. This
means that the model is not complex enough to describe the data. A further
challenge with ML is that its results can be thought of as opaque or a “black

box,” producing outcomes based on relationships that are not readily
explainable.
ML typically requires vast amounts of data. A typical process begins with a
training dataset, in which the model looks for relationships. A validation dataset
is then used to refine these connections, which can be applied to a test dataset to
analyze its predictive ability. The training set is the largest of the three datasets,
including around 60%–80% of the total data available (typically, for larger
datasets, the percentage will be toward the upper end of this range; for smaller
datasets, it will be toward the lower end). The validation and test datasets split
the remaining 20%–40% of the data evenly.
Data are allocated randomly among the three datasets to reduce bias and the risk
of overfitting, and to help prevent data leakage, which is information from
outside the training dataset influencing the model’s learning. However, with time
series data that rely on chronological order to be interpreted accurately,
allocating randomly among the three datasets would lose underlying patterns and
dependencies within the data. This also reopens the algorithm to data leakage if a
later piece of data (which has only occurred because of earlier data) ends up in
the training dataset. Two methods of allocating time series data are time-based
splits and rolling-window validations.
Time-based split. The data are simply split in chronological order. The earliest
60%–80% of data is used in the training dataset, the next 10%–20% in the
validation dataset, and the most recent 10%–20% in the testing dataset.
Rolling-window validation. This first trains the model on an initial portion of
the period covered (e.g., January to July), validates it on a later period (e.g.,
September and October), and then goes back toward the beginning and trains
on another dataset (e.g., February to August), thus “rolling the window” along.
Regardless of which method is chosen to allocate time series data, the period
covered across the validation and test datasets should match the intended
forecast horizon. For example, if an analyst wishes to forecast for the next two
years, the algorithm needs to have been able to learn what patterns are presented
over a two-year period.
Human expertise is required to ensure an appropriate model is selected and to
ensure that the input data are reliable, have been cleaned (fixing or removing any
errors in the original data), and minimize any biases. Expertise is also required to
interpret and appropriately act on the model’s predictions and suggestions.

Neural Networks
For nonlinear relationships with many interdependencies, neural networks may
be the most suitable form of ML. These are inspired by biological neural
systems, and they have many layers of interconnected nodes (known as neurons)
through which the data are processed to find patterns.
Neural networks begin with an initial or input layer that receives raw data, much
like the other types of ML models, and they can engage in supervised or
unsupervised learning. They have many hidden, or intermediate, layers that
process this information and produce neurons to represent each different variable
or characteristic, with the idea that the input data may link to these variables
through several layers. Each layer has weights assigned to the different neurons,
depending on their importance.
Neural networks can be trained through backpropagation, a form of supervised
learning. During training, the data move through each layer, and an initial
prediction is made. This prediction is compared to the actual outcome, a process
known as a forward pass. Next, the neural network quantifies the error and
calculates the loss. The objective of backpropagation is to minimize this loss.
Once the loss has been calculated, the network tests to see how much a change in
weights of the different neurons affects the error, known as the loss gradient.
These weights are adjusted gradually (known as the gradient descent) to reduce
the loss gradient as much as possible. This process repeats many times to
improve the accuracy of the prediction. The model’s task is to identify all these
different links and apply appropriate weights before reaching the output, or final,
layer where a prediction can be made.
More complex types of neural networks include generative adversarial
networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders (VAEs).
GANs combine two separate neural networks, a generator network and a
discriminator network, to produce realistic synthetic data in a comparable way
to how an analyst might use a spreadsheet to produce scenarios to stress test.
The training is performed on historic market data, with the aim of producing
plausible future scenarios. Though this can be helpful, one must review the use
of any output of GANs carefully because they can be used to create highly
realistic fake material.

VAEs start by compressing data into a compact form, then trying to reconstruct
the data. This is often used in finance to reduce dimensionality and improve
efficiency in analyzing large sets of financial data without compromising on
pattern recognition, and it can assist in identifying anomalies. This is a form of
probabilistic generative model, using encoder and decoder networks.
A more traditional way of analyzing nonlinear relationships is using copulas.
These are mathematical functions, such as the Cholesky decomposition, which
use marginal probability distributions to identify dependencies between random
variables.
Neural networks are expected to increase in use within finance as technical
capabilities improve and become more accessible, reducing the associated cost.
Natural Language Processing and Large Language Models
AI was initially created to perform tasks such as pattern recognition and
decision-making in a faster and more accurate way than humans. In finance, this
can be used to analyze qualitative as well as quantitative data.
Natural language processing (NLP) refers to the use of computers and AI to
interpret human language. Speech recognition and language translation are
among the uses of NLP. Possible applications in finance could be to check for
regulatory compliance in examining employee communications, or to evaluate
large volumes of research reports to detect more subtle changes in sentiment
than can be discerned from analysts’ recommendations alone.
For text analytics, the input is typically unstructured and in the form of writing
(company filings, written reports) or voice recordings (quarterly earnings calls,
surveys). NLP can translate these into a usable format much faster than humanly
possible, while looking for patterns. Lexical analysis may also be used to
analyze characteristics, such as word frequency.
Large language models (LLMs) are a form of generative AI that generate real-
world scenarios in a human-like format. LLMs use neural networks to identify
context and meaning within qualitative input data, such as a collection of market
and company information. Nonfinancial input data, such as information on
political polls for an upcoming election, can also have a significant impact on the
finance-focused qualitative output. The output is human-like text covering the
relevant topic, such as a summary of the input data or a performance forecast

based on the tone and sentiment of the input data. This is typically achieved
through self-supervised learning, a form of unsupervised learning where the
model creates its own labels for unlabeled input data and corrects its assigned
weights as it learns. Training must first take place on a vast dataset to ensure the
model learns the appropriate linguistics, such as semantics and grammar, as well
as accurately interpreting finance-specific terminology.
One of the risks of LLMs is that, while they are well practiced in producing
human-like text and predicting word patterns, they are not designed to assess or
identify errors in financial data. Analysts must review the output with a
skeptical, expert eye. To ensure accuracy, analysts should use LLMs alongside
more traditional data-driven models.
Programming languages used in financial data science include the following:
Python. This is the basis for many fintech apps.
R. This is used for statistical analysis.
Java. This is used for many internet apps and can be run from different
computers, servers, or operating systems concurrently.
C/C++. This is a specialized, high-speed programming language that is used
for algorithmic and high-frequency trading.
Some of the databases used are SQL (structured, on a server), SQLite (structured,
not on a server, most frequently used for mobile apps that require access to data),
and NoSQL (for unstructured data).
MODULE QUIZ 11.1
1. In contrast with traditional data sources used in finance, which of the following is most
likely classified as an alternative data source? A company’s:
A. annual report.
B. banking records.
C. regulatory filings.
2. In machine learning, which of the following datasets is most likely to use the largest
proportion of the underlying data?
A. Test dataset.
B. Training dataset.
C. Validation dataset.
3. Underfitting is most accurately described as treating:
A. noise as noise.
B. noise as true parameters.

C. true parameters as noise.
4. In neural networks, the purpose of backpropagation is to:
A. train the model by using a system of rewards and penalties.
B. ensure data privacy is protected and other regulations are upheld.
C. minimize the difference between the predicted and actual outcome.
KEY CONCEPTS
LOS 11.a
Financial data science is the quantitative and qualitative analysis of financial
information. Fintech refers to developments in technology that can be applied to
the financial services industry.
Big data refers to the vast amount of information produced that could be useful
for analysis, including data from traditional and alternative sources.
Characteristics of financial big data include its volume, velocity, variety, and
veracity.
Data science includes appropriate approaches to the capture, curation, storage,
search, and transfer of data to the appropriate model being used for analysis, as
well as consideration of how the results should be presented.
Data mining focuses on identifying patterns from large datasets, which can then
be used to predict outputs.
AI refers to computer systems that can be programmed to simulate human
cognition. Machine learning (ML) and neural networks are examples of AI.
ML is programming that gives a computer system the ability to improve its
performance of a task over time and is often used to detect patterns in large sets
of data. The model can be trained using supervised or unsupervised learning.
Some models will use reinforcement learning to improve their output.
ML splits data into three datasets: training (the largest), validation, and test. Data
can be allocated randomly among these three, but with time-series data, more
sophisticated allocation techniques such as time-based split and rolling-window
validations should be used.
Key risks of data mining and ML are overfitting, where a model misinterprets
noise as important, and underfitting, where a model misinterprets important
information as noise.

Neural networks are used for nonlinear relationships. Starting with an input
layer, there are then several hidden layers which link the variables to each other
in a non-linear fashion, before reaching the output layer. Backpropagation is
used to improve the accuracy of the output by calculating the loss and loss
gradients, then changing the weights of each neuron to minimize the loss.
Applications of fintech to investment management include text analytics, natural
language processing, risk governance, and algorithmic trading.
ANSWER KEY FOR MODULE QUIZZES
Module Quiz 11.1
. B Data generated from business processes, such as banking and sales records,
are considered alternative data. Financial reports and regulatory filings are
traditional sources of data. (LOS 11.a)
. B The training dataset comprises 60%–80% of the data available. The
validation and test datasets each comprise 10%–20%. (LOS 11.a)
. C Underfitting occurs when the machine fails to identify actual patterns and
relationships, treating true parameters as noise. Treating noise as true
parameters is overfitting. (LOS 11.a)
. C Neural networks can be trained through backpropagation, where an initial
prediction is compared to the actual outcome. The neural network will
quantify this error and calculate the loss (the loss gradient) before changing
the weights of different neurons to reduce the difference as much as
possible. Reinforcement learning trains the model through a system of
rewards and penalties. While it is important that data privacy is protected
and other regulations are upheld, this is not related to backpropagation.
(LOS 11.a)
